finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the dba role check is never enforced. Any caller can drop tables. The vacuum handler checks the error correctly, which shows the check was intended.
finding.source: Any HTTP client calling POST /admin/drop, with any user lacking the 'dba' role

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered directly, with no auth middleware
userFrom gets the user from the request context
Authorize's return value is discarded, so a 'forbidden' error does not stop the handler
The DROP TABLE statement runs regardless of the role check

finding.guards_checked: Authorize only returns an error and never writes a response. dropTable has no early return. No middleware is registered in main. The sibling handler vacuum at lines 33-36 checks the error, so dropTable differs from it.

verdict.guard_found: api.go:22 userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on r.Context().Value("user"). Nothing in the codebase sets that value, so the assertion panics on nil before Authorize or runSQL runs. net/http recovers the panic and aborts the request.
verdict.reason: The discarded Authorize error at api.go:26 is real, but the DROP at api.go:27 is unreachable as written: no code sets the "user" context value (the only match for "user" or WithValue is api.go:22), so the non-comma-ok assertion at api.go:22 panics on every request to /admin/drop before the sink runs. The missing check would only become exploitable if an auth middleware were added that populates the user.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the unsanitized form value 't' is concatenated into a DROP TABLE statement. Even with a working authorization check, a caller could inject extra SQL. Because of F1, no role is needed to reach this.
finding.source: The 't' parameter, read with r.FormValue("t") (query string or POST body)

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated directly into the SQL string
runSQL is a stub in this file, but its argument is a raw SQL string, so the injection is real if it is implemented as an executor

finding.guards_checked: There is no identifier allowlist, quoting or validation. Parameterized queries cannot be used for identifiers. Combined with F1, any caller can reach this.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose error is discarded, so it blocks nothing (contrast vacuum at api.go:33). No allowlist, quoting or parameterization on 't'.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " with no validation, and the only guard at api.go:26 ignores its returned error, so any caller of /admin/drop (api.go:44) reaches it; runSQL is only a stub at api.go:41, so exploitability assumes a real executor.

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the request context value. If no authentication middleware sets the "user" key, the assertion panics. In this file no middleware sets it, so requests to the admin endpoints panic, which net/http recovers per request. This is a robustness and availability issue, and the auth setup is incomplete.

trace.note: Handlers are registered without any middleware that populates the context
The single-value type assertion panics when the value is nil

finding.guards_checked: No comma-ok form is used and no middleware exists in this repository. Whether auth middleware exists elsewhere is unknown, because this is the only file.

verdict.guard_found: none (no middleware in api.go; net/http's per-request panic recovery contains the crash)
verdict.reason: api.go:22 does a single-value `.(*User)` assertion, and api.go:44-45 register the admin handlers with no context-populating middleware, so any anonymous request panics at api.go:25/32. The panic is recovered per request and fails closed, because it happens before the `runSQL` calls at api.go:27 and 37. The impact is limited to robustness and noisy logs, which is what the claim says. Separately, api.go:26 discards Authorize's result, which would be a real authorization bypass if middleware were added.
